If antivirals are used they should be started early in the prodromal phase. Topical antivirals, including aciclovir, penciclovir, and tromantadine, have been used and are most effective when started during the prodromal phase.3 Docosanol may be a further alternative for topi- cal use.4 Oral antivirals (aciclovir, famciclovir, and val- aciclovir) may shorten the duration of symptomatic le- sions by about 1 day.3 High-dose oral valaciclovir has also been reported to be effective for suppression of re- currences and may provide the convenience of single- day treatment.5 In immunocompromised patients with primary symptomatic infection or recurrent episodes of infection, intravenous or oral aciclovir, oral famciclovir, or valaciclovir may be used. An oral antiviral (aciclovir, famciclovir, or valaciclovir) is recommended for pa- tients with herpes labialis and concurrent HIV infec- tion.6 • Genital herpes is usually treated with oral aciclovir, famciclovir, or valaciclovir.6-9 Intravenous aciclovir is given for severe disease or neurological complications. A study10 found that both oral aciclovir and oral valaci- clovir were effective in suppressing the frequency of re- currences and amount of HSV shedding. However, treatment of the primary HSV infection appears to have no effect on subsequent recurrences. Symptomatic re- currences in patients with a recognisable prodrome may be aborted or the severity reduced by a 5-day course of oral aciclovir, famciclovir, or valaciclovir begun by the patient.7-9 Alternative regimens include high oral doses of aciclovir for 2 days,8,11 famciclovir for 1 day, or val- aciclovir for 3 days.7,8 Symptomatic HSV recurrences in HIV-positive patients respond more slowly to anti- HSV treatment and longer treatment courses and higher doses of antivirals are needed.8,12 In HIV-negative patients without a prodrome, or those with frequent recurrences, continuous suppressive ther- apy with aciclovir, famciclovir, or valaciclovir should be considered.7-9 Once-daily suppressive therapy with valaciclovir was found to significantly reduce the risk of transmission of genital herpes among heterosexual, HSV-2-discordant couples.13 Suppressive therapy should be considered for all HIV-infected persons.7,12 • Ocular herpes simplex infections usually require treatment with antivirals and/or interferons. Topical an- tivirals include aciclovir, ganciclovir, trifluridine, and vidarabine; no one drug appears to be more effective than another.14 Systemic antivirals include aciclovir, famciclovir, and valaciclovir.
